title: Clustering on a Network

source.pdf_page_offset_note: Physical page 1 is an unnumbered Summary; physical pages 2-34 are internally numbered 1-33.

notes: All 34 text pages and all 34 rendered pages were reviewed in order by the root thread and three independent read-only page-range audits.
Seven full-range JPEG contact proxies and one formula crop stayed below 450000 bytes; no original full-page PNG or multi-image tool result entered model context.

context_sources.summary: VHF propagation, duplex repeaters, and amateur-radio practice motivate the range and frequency abstractions.
SEDAC population imagery supplies a qualitative comparison for the clumped generator.
Ten references cover population data, radio practice, frequency allocation, clustering, propagation, and operator procedure.

inputs: 1,000 potential users in a radius-40-mile flat circular domain
145-148 MHz band, 600 kHz repeater offsets, and 54 privacy lines
user request rate, local-call bias, handheld and repeater ranges
outputs: adaptation sketches for 10,000 users and mountainous terrain
decisions: minimum feasible repeater infrastructure under a chosen service threshold
where to place repeaters and connectors
how to route simultaneous branch traffic
when the design is outside its tested regime

section_map.summary: The Summary states the 40-mile circular-domain task, the 145-148 MHz band, the 1,000-user interpretation, density-aware repeater placement, privacy-line routing, k-means centroids, component connection, clumped-population tests, coverage and capacity metrics, a 98 percent result, a 32 percent naive comparison, and a high-load subnetwork boundary.

The title and two-page contents expose the complete sequence from technical background and assumptions through metrics, placement and routing algorithms, results, 10,000-user and terrain adaptations, limitations, appendix figures, and references.

The Introduction moves from VHF line-of-sight and duplex repeaters through CTCSS interference control to the optimization task, then operationally redefines simultaneous users as a population that may generate requests at a parameterized rate.

Nine assumptions define radial coverage, touching-range connectivity, negligible propagation time, 9-mile repeater and 3-mile handheld ranges, polite users, queued conflicts, 600 kHz spacing, equal load, United States regulation, and strongly local call demand.

The metric section defines accommodation as the fraction Q of attempted transmissions processed and gives a timestep queue simulation in which uncovered endpoints fail, noninterfering requests begin, conflicts wait, and leftover requests fail at the horizon.

The request generator biases communication toward short tower paths with a displayed finite formula, while overall quality prioritizes the smallest repeater count subject to a configurable capacity threshold and secondary coverage or demand checks.

Population synthesis replaces an independent uniform sample with random clump centers and an independent-coordinate Gaussian-like field using sigma_x=sigma_y=20, then visually compares random, 5, 10, 20, and 40-clump patterns with one southeastern United States density image.

The linking section rejects reciprocal two-repeater frequencies because of feedback, defines A through E staggered 600 kHz receive-transmit pairs, adds inverse repeaters for bidirectionality, and sketches a weak-power continuation for chains longer than five levels.

The naive baseline blankets the circle with evenly spaced connected repeaters, removes nodes covering nobody, and is rejected because it wastes sparse-area nodes, risks feedback or one-way links, and turns most communication into a single whole-network broadcast.

The privacy-line section introduces a central hub, inward and outward directions, branch-local traffic, paired destination labels, a worked 6/13-to-8/15 route, and line 54 as a stop signal before generalizing which lines each repeater accepts.

The k-means section groups nearby users, places repeaters at cluster centroids, and wraps clustering, range construction, component connection, adjacency construction, and channel assignment into the Main Network Generation Algorithm.

Disconnected repeater components become graph nodes weighted by their nearest intercomponent separation; the paper invokes a minimum spanning tree idea and repeatedly adds a repeater toward the closest other component until the network is connected.

The channel algorithm chooses the node with greatest closeness centrality as hub, maps levels 1-5 to A, B/A-prime, C/B-prime, D/C-prime, and E/D-prime, then assigns increasing channel numbers by an outward breadth-first traversal.

The experiment crosses five population types with five initial cluster counts and five generated populations per type, then reports mean repeater counts, uncovered users, and ten-run transmission-capacity variability against the naive network.

Tables 3 and 4 report capacity standard deviations and mean processed-request proportions, showing a large clustering advantage over the naive network but also nonmonotone cells and a repeater-count versus capacity tradeoff.

The Discussion explains the 10,000-user hub bottleneck, proposes recursively isolated local subnetworks and multiple hubs, and adapts placement and component connection to mountainous terrain through asymmetric ranges and simulated annealing.

The Conclusion relies on an eyeball test and tables to claim shape adaptation, high coverage, high throughput, and relatively few wasteful nodes, while restricting the feasible search to cluster counts compatible with the finite privacy-line budget.

The limitations section records k-means nondeterminism, duplicate delayed signals, the roughly 25-location privacy-line cap, missing cost tradeoffs, weather sensitivity, indirect repeater-count control, blind interference, switching time, heterogeneous demand, and a greedy removal extension.

Appendix Figures 6-8 show repeated network instances for random and 5, 10, 20, and 40-clump populations, followed by ten references for population data, VHF practice, frequency allocation, clustering, propagation, and operator procedures.

assumptions.summary: The 1,000 users are potential requesters rather than simultaneous transmitters.
Handheld and repeater broadcasts are radially symmetric in a flat circular domain.
Touching repeater broadcast radii imply mutual communication.
Radio propagation and required buffers are negligible at the simulation timestep.
Repeaters reach about 9 miles and handheld users reach about 3 miles for network access.
Licensed users listen, cooperate, and do not initiate a local request while a tower is busy.
Long-chain conflicts wait in a queue instead of failing immediately.
A 600 kHz offset is an adequate minimum distinction between repeater frequency stages.
Every user imposes approximately equal demand.
The network is deployed under United States amateur-radio rules.
Calls are strongly biased toward short repeater paths.
Population coordinates can be generated by independent x and y clumps with sigma_x=sigma_y=20.
A tree-like hub and destination privacy lines can control signal direction.
K-means centroids are useful proxies for high-density repeater locations.
Closeness centrality selects a low-load-path hub and breadth-first levels remain frequency feasible.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: The user population is interpreted as potential requesters with an average request parameter.
Requests are scheduled by timestep with source, destination, and network assignment.
Request distance is biased toward shorter repeater paths by the displayed source formula with lambda=1.
Population generators choose random clump centers and independent coordinate draws with sigma_x=sigma_y=20.
Synthetic fields are compared qualitatively with one actual southeastern United States density image.
K-means converts user positions into cluster memberships and centroid repeater positions.
Repeater adjacency is partitioned into connected components and reduced to nearest intercomponent distances.
Five populations per type and ten capacity simulations per network populate the result tables.

models.summary: Estimate a radio horizon in miles from antenna height in feet using the paper's displayed rule.
Measure the fraction of attempted transmissions processed during the simulation.
Retain the displayed request-distance expression exactly for audit; the paper sets lambda=1 but does not define k.
Represent the source's printed population field without silently inserting a missing negative exponent.
Weight the component graph by its closest pair of repeaters.
Place the next connector along the direction between the closest disconnected repeaters.
Receive on one frequency and rebroadcast 600 kHz away while using a subaudible tone to gate activation.
Represent each handheld and repeater by a circular range and infer adjacency from touching or overlapping ranges.
Delay conflicting long-chain requests rather than counting them as immediate failures.
Generate requests, step through time, greedily accept noninterfering transmissions, fail uncovered endpoints, and count leftovers.
Search the algorithm's feasible repeater counts for the smallest network meeting a chosen Q threshold and inspect coverage and demand robustness.
Choose random clump centers and sample independent x and y coordinates around them, with sigma_x=sigma_y=20.
Assign A through E receive-transmit pairs so each repeater's output is the next repeater's input.
Co-locate inverse repeater types with forward types to create reverse propagation along a chain.
Use a weak E-prime bridge with D/D-prime and continue backward through C/C-prime and B/B-prime for chains beyond five levels.
Tile the circular area with connected repeaters and remove only nodes that cover no users.
Route signals inward to a hub and outward to one destination branch using paired location labels and a stop line.
Cluster users by Euclidean proximity and use each cluster centroid as an initial repeater position.
Compose clustering, repeater ranges, component connection, adjacency construction, and channel assignment.
Treat disconnected components as nodes and choose low-separation links intended to minimize added connection length.
Repeatedly find the closest pair of disconnected repeaters and add an intermediate repeater toward the other component.
Choose the repeater with smallest average geodesic distance to other network nodes.
Assign channel 1 to the hub and increasing channel numbers to successive outward adjacency layers.
Evaluate five population types, five cluster counts, and five generated populations per type, with ten request simulations for capacity.
Count initial centroid repeaters plus connectors and compare means across population and cluster settings.
Count users outside every repeater range and compare the clustering network with the 100-percent-cover baseline.
Repeat the request simulation ten times and report the mean processed fraction and its standard deviation.
Recursively add frequency-incompatible local subnetworks at high-demand nodes to isolate local traffic.
Replace symmetric ranges with position-dependent adjacency, then refine clustered and connecting repeater positions by simulated annealing.
Enumerate cluster counts compatible with the privacy-line budget and choose the first network meeting the capacity requirement.
Remove the repeater whose deletion causes the least quality reduction until the requested count is reached.

verification.limitation: No common scale, metric, or fitted goodness-of-fit test is supplied.

verification.summary: The uniformly blanketed network is retained as a naive comparator.
verification.strength: Makes the capacity cost of whole-network broadcasting visible.
verification.limitation: It is not tuned under the same repeater-count or service constraints.

verification.summary: Five independently generated populations are used for each of five population types.
verification.limitation: Five replicates are small and random seeds are absent.

verification.summary: Table 1 reports mean repeater counts with variability for five cluster counts.

verification.limitation: No cost or statistical interval is attached.

verification.summary: Table 2 reports mean uncovered-user counts and includes the zero-uncovered naive baseline.
verification.strength: Prevents capacity gains from hiding coverage loss.

verification.strength: Separates stochastic request variability from mean performance.

verification.summary: The 10,000-user stress case is used to expose a central-hub bottleneck.

verification.summary: Appendix Figures 6-8 show multiple network instances for each population-clump regime.

results_trace.summary: The Summary reports up to 98 percent processed transmissions for the clustering network versus a maximum of 32 percent for the naive network.
Table 1 shows repeater counts rising with cluster count; for random populations the mean grows from 17.00 at 5 clusters to 74.60 at 25 clusters.
Table 2 shows uncovered random users falling from 382.20 at 5 clusters to 7.80 at 25 clusters, while the naive network has zero uncovered users.
Table 3 reports capacity standard deviations from 0.0033 to 0.0144 for k-means and 0.0065 to 0.0083 for the naive network.
Table 4 reports clustering processed-request fractions from 0.621 to 0.985 depending on cluster count and population, versus 0.221 to 0.313 for naive.
The best clustering cells are not monotone in every column; 5-clump capacity declines from 0.850 at 10 clusters to 0.814 at 25 clusters.
For 10,000 users the paper reports roughly half the requests handled by networks with 15-20 repeaters, versus about 700 of 10,000 for naive.
The conclusion highlights a 15-cluster setting as more than 97 percent coverage and about 95 percent capacity with roughly 40 repeaters, although the table cells vary by population.

contributions.summary: Defines a simulation-based processed-request service ratio.
Builds staggered forward and inverse repeater chains inside the band.
Uses hub-oriented privacy labels to localize branch traffic.
Combines k-means population placement with graph connection.
Selects a closeness-centrality hub and assigns channels outward.
Evaluates infrastructure, coverage, stochastic capacity, and a naive comparator together.

writing_logic.summary: Summary chain: radio-network task -> density placement -> privacy routing -> clustering and component connection -> synthetic tests -> capacity contrast -> high-load boundary.
Introduction chain: VHF range -> duplex repeaters -> interference and CTCSS -> official task -> operational user interpretation.
Assumption chain: propagation and range -> cooperative users -> simplified conflict handling -> spectrum spacing -> local demand.
Metric chain: service meaning -> Q ratio -> queue simulation -> configurable threshold -> smallest-network objective.
Population chain: reject uniform independence -> generate clumps -> display a Gaussian-like field -> compare synthetic and actual images.
Frequency chain: reject reciprocal feedback -> stagger A-E -> add inverse types -> sketch extended chains.
Routing chain: expose naive broadcast bottleneck -> introduce hub direction -> work one destination-label path -> generalize branch-local rules.
Construction chain: k-means centroids -> repeater ranges -> connect components -> adjacency -> centrality hub -> breadth-first channels.
Evaluation chain: experiment cells -> repeater counts -> uncovered users -> capacity variability -> mean capacity -> resource-service tradeoff.
Boundary chain: 10,000-user bottleneck -> proposed subnetworks -> terrain adaptation -> conclusion -> nondeterminism, radio, budget, and objective limitations.

language_observations.summary: The Summary gives methods, tests, comparator, numerical headline, and limitations in a compact five-paragraph progression.
Technical background repeatedly uses mechanism-to-consequence sentences before introducing the modeling task.
For the purpose of this problem marks an explicit reinterpretation of an ambiguous requirement.
Assumptions are justified one by one with a physical or operational rationale, even when the rationale is incomplete.
A rhetorical question about what users want is converted into a measurable processed-request ratio.
A concrete feedback failure motivates the staggered frequency scheme before the A-E list appears.
After a long routing example, the phrase let us review the core idea compresses it into general forwarding rules.
Algorithm prose uses Require, Ensure, named intermediate arrays, and explicit handoffs to the next procedure.
Results paragraphs move from table variability to performance contrast and then to a repeater-capacity tradeoff.
The conclusion uses strong adjectives, then the future-work section partially retracts them through nondeterminism and engineering limits.

visualization_observations.summary: Provides the complete task-method-test-comparison-limit contract before the main paper.
Exposes the ordering from Introduction through Results and the method subsections.
Exposes Discussion, Conclusion, Future Work, and Appendix handoffs.
Makes queue order, uncovered failures, conflict deferral, and horizon leftovers inspectable.

visualization_observations.figure: Figure 1 synthetic and actual population distributions
visualization_observations.summary: Compares random and four clumped generators with one real density image.
Shows the uniformly blanketed baseline and its redundant coverage geometry.
Shows hub branches, repeater types, paired location labels, and directed line semantics.
Connects colored user clusters to centroid-based repeater placement.
Shows the closest-component loop and the bridge-spacing expression.
Maps channel levels 1-5 to forward and inverse repeater types.
Shows closeness-hub selection and breadth-first outward assignment.
Quantifies infrastructure growth across cluster counts and population types.
Quantifies the coverage cost of fewer clusters against the naive baseline.
Separates simulation variability from mean capacity.
Provides the principal clustering-versus-naive capacity comparison and nonmonotone cells.
Shows the proposed three-repeater local augmentation beside the unaugmented network.
Shows instance-to-instance network geometry for random and 5, 10, 20, and 40-clump populations.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: A summary with a quantitative comparator plausibly improves traceability but does not establish optimality.
Four explicit algorithms plausibly make the design easier to audit despite interface defects.
Joint reporting of repeater count, coverage, and capacity plausibly improves decision relevance when tradeoffs are not hidden.

weaknesses.summary: The printed horizon rule is distance=sqrt(1.5 h); it differs from the commonly cited coefficient-times-square-root form and gives about 7.75 miles at 40 feet rather than the later 9-mile value.
The paper redefines 1,000 simultaneous users as 1,000 possible requesters with a parameterized average rate, materially weakening the original concurrency interpretation.
CTCSS or a privacy tone gates repeater activation but does not by itself prevent two simultaneous radio signals from physically interfering.
The claimed one-to-two-second delay is not attributable to radio-wave propagation across an 80-mile domain; equipment and protocol delay are not separately modeled.
Downlink and handheld uplink ranges are asymmetric, yet coverage and communication feasibility are treated largely through circular reach without a complete link-budget rule.
The model deliberately queues conflicting requests instead of counting them as failed, so interference is less heavily penalized than the paper's own service definition suggests.
A 600 kHz duplex offset is treated as a minimum distinguishable channel spacing without a spectrum plan, occupied bandwidth, adjacent-channel, or regulatory analysis.
The assumption that users listen on all privacy lines for several minutes before every request is operationally implausible and leaves an unresolved CITE placeholder.
Q omits waiting time, fairness, transmission duration, hop count, repeated retries, and the distribution of service across users.
Algorithm 1 is order-dependent because it greedily scans the queue; no randomization, priority policy, fairness diagnostic, or maximum waiting time is defined.
The interference predicate used by Algorithm 1 is not formalized, so the simulation cannot be reproduced from the pseudocode alone.

The request-distance expression is called Poisson but contains a binomial coefficient, an undefined k, l factorial, and a binomial-like final term; it is neither a standard Poisson PMF nor a fully defined alternative.
The claimed lower bound is only a lower bound within networks generated by this heuristic and does not establish a global minimum repeater count.
The printed population field has a positive quadratic exponent and no negative one-half factor, so it is not a normalizable bivariate Gaussian density.
The paper does not explain how Gaussian samples outside the radius-40 circle are rejected, truncated, wrapped, or resampled.
Figure 1 compares synthetic coordinate plots with an actual density image using different color systems, scales, and no common units, so the claimed similarity is qualitative.
Five staggered 600 kHz pairs across 145-148 MHz use band-edge values but do not document occupied bandwidth, repeater coordination, or whether all pairings are legally deployable.
The weak E-prime extension, simultaneous-shutdown rule, and timeout behavior have no power threshold, delay model, stability proof, or simulation.
The privacy-line routing example assumes effectively instantaneous duplicate forwarding and postpones the resulting offset-signal collision to the limitations section.
Line 54 is used as a stop signal without a complete allocation and reuse rule across the whole network.
Algorithm 2 alternates MaximumRepeaterRange, MaximumRegionRange, RepeaterRanges, and UserRanges, leaving its input-output interface inconsistent.
K-means minimizes within-cluster squared distance, not uncovered users, repeater count, interference, or network capacity, so centroid placement is only a heuristic for the stated objective.
A minimum-total-distance spanning plan over components does not necessarily minimize the number of added repeaters when ranges and required integer connectors matter.
Algorithm 3 does not define the ceiling rule for numRepeatersRequired and its repeated closest-component procedure is asserted to be an MST without a complete proof.
Algorithm 4 does not reconcile graph depths beyond channel 5 with the extended-chain construction and does not verify channel compatibility on cycles or multi-parent layers.
The five generated populations per population type are too few for stable uncertainty estimates, and no random seeds or reproducible code are supplied.
The statement that more initial clusters increase capacity is not generally monotone: several 5-clump and 10-clump table entries decline as clusters increase.
The claim that even the 5-clump standard deviation is below 1.5 percent conflicts with displayed values such as 0.102 and 0.074 if table entries are proportions.
Table 4 is captioned as a percentage but reports fractions between zero and one, inviting a factor-100 interpretation error.
The recursive subnetwork feature is explicitly unfinished and unevaluated, and the text points to Figure 4 although the comparison is Figure 5.
The mountainous-terrain extension gives no propagation model, elevation data interface, asymmetric distance definition, objective function, annealing schedule, or experiment.
The conclusion's 15-cluster claim of over 97 percent coverage and about 95 percent transmission is not uniform across population types; the 5-clump capacity entry is only 0.830.
The claimed maximum of roughly 25 distinct locations and the typical network of about 40 repeaters require a co-location accounting rule that is not explicitly reconciled.
The privacy-line count leading to the 25-location cap is not derived in a complete allocation table, and duplicate processing delays are not quantified.
The greedy repeater-removal proposal depends on an undefined network-quality loss and has no optimality, complexity, or connectivity guarantee.

independent_extensions.summary: Replace range rules with a calibrated bidirectional link budget, terrain profile, fading margin, and regulatory channel plan.
Use an event-driven queue with durations, maximum waits, priorities, fairness, and a tested interference graph.
Fit a truncated or bounded spatial mixture model to measured population data and validate it quantitatively.
Optimize a multi-objective network over repeater cost, uncovered demand, capacity, robustness, and spectrum feasibility rather than k-means distance alone.
Formulate connector cost as required integer repeaters and solve channel assignment with explicit cycle, depth, and interference constraints.
Publish code and seeds, use more replicates, report uncertainty, fix a service threshold, and compare Pareto-efficient networks.

candidate_rule_impacts.action: retain task-method-metric-comparator language only when strong adjectives remain tied to exact test cells and uncertainty
treat population coordinates, repeater geometry, adjacency, spectrum state, and terrain as versioned measured data rather than anonymous arrays
retain a ledger for range, frequency, offset, privacy lines, request rate, cluster count, sigma, simulation horizon, and service threshold
retain graph and spatial heuristics only after units, topology, radio mechanism, objective, and calibration agree
combine repeater count, coverage, capacity, waiting, and interference through a declared decision rule rather than a favorable table narrative
keep user count, simultaneous transmissions, repeater count, distinct locations, coverage, capacity, variability, and decisions separately labeled
stress geometric placement and hub choices under perturbed populations, ranges, seeds, terrains, and channel budgets
make reliability population-, load-, spectrum-, terrain-, and queue-policy-specific with uncertainty and abstention outside the tested regime
run a mathematical and algorithmic preflight on the horizon rule, request expression, Gaussian sign, connector rounding, variable names, and channel depth before simulation
retain network and population maps only with common axes, scale, legends, node and edge semantics, coverage meaning, and linked numeric metrics
choose distance computation, centrality, connectivity, and caching from measured graph size, query volume, update rate, memory, and accuracy needs
